newsitem.title: USA: United Carolina offer on high end - analysts.
newsitem.headline: United Carolina offer on high end - analysts.

text.p: Southern National Corp's $985-million offer for United Carolina Bancshares Corp was on the high end, analysts said on Monday.
But the deal would yield enormous savings, analysts said, citing an overlap in branch offices, as the two North Carolina banks operate in many of the same locales in the Carolinas.
"It was a full price but one would assume that there are pretty significant opportunites to trim the fat and that makes it a little more rational," said Darren Short of The Robinson-Humphrey Co.

"Typically when a bank acquires another and they have significant overlap, that portends significant cost savings from branch consolidation, head count reductions and back office redundancies," Short said.
The banks did not detail any of that information but were due to further discuss the offer in a teleconference with reporters on Monday.
Southern National operates 425 banking offices in 219 cities throughout the Carolinas and Virginia. United Carolina Bancshares (UCB) operates 153 offices in 89 communities in the Carolinas.
The banks announced earlier Monday that their boards of directors unanimously approved the deal at $40.01 per share.

Whiteville, N.C.-based UCB's shares would each be exchanged for 1.135 shares of Winston-Salem, N.C.-based Southern National stock. In mid morning trading shares of Southern National were down 1-1/2 to 33-3/4 on the New York Stock Exchange while UCB's shares soared 9-3/8 to 36-7/8.
If the deal were approved, Southern National's deposits would climb from $15 billion to top $19 billion, surpassing Wachovia Corp to hold the biggest share of deposits in the state.
It would trail banking giants NationsBank Corp and First Union Corp in overall size, however because their out-of-state operations extend along the East Coast.
The merger between Southern National and UCB would form a financial institution with more than $25 billion in assets, the banks said. It is due to be completed next year.

UCB would be the first of the state's midsized banks, hampered by competitive problems with consumer services, to agree to a buyout. Customers of the midsized banks cannot match the huge automated teller machine networks or mutual fund offerings put forth by NationsBank and First Union.
"This deal will force even greater takeover speculation regarding those size companies," said David West of Davenport & Co.

Added Christopher Marinac of Interstate/Johnson Lane: "Over the next two to three years boards of directors of mid- sized banks will need to make the case why they should stay independent. They will be vulnerable because economies of scale are being driven by size."
